title: FOLD PAPER
42 TIMES?

script.beat: 1 HOOK (0-3 s): the title's promise, with the number, subject already moving
script.text: Fold a sheet of paper forty-two times, and it reaches the Moon.

script.beat: 2 SETUP: the hypothetical, labelled, then the two facts it rests on
script.text: Imagine it. Paper is a tenth of a millimeter thick. Every fold doubles the stack.
Ten folds? As tall as a mug. Thirty folds? Past the edge of space.

script.beat: 4 EVIDENCE: the number, as a picture
script.text: Forty-two folds make four trillion layers, over four hundred thousand kilometers tall.
Here's the catch. By hand, about seven folds is the limit. The record is twelve.

script.beat: 6 PAYOFF + LOOP: reframes the hook, echoes the opening
script.text: So paper can reach the Moon. You just can't fold it that far.

science.claim: A sheet of paper is about a tenth of a millimeter thick.
science.source: Live Science, 'How many times can you fold a piece of paper in half?'

science.claim: Forty-two folds make over four trillion layers, over four hundred thousand kilometers tall.
science.working: 2^42 = 4,398,046,511,104 layers. x 0.1 mm = 4.398e11 mm = 439,805 km. The Moon's average distance is about 384,400 km, so the stack is past it. 2^41 = 219,902 km is not, so 42 is the first fold that gets there.
science.status: arithmetic checked; re-check the Moon distance on nasa.gov before publishing

science.claim: Ten folds is as tall as a mug; thirty folds is past the edge of space.
science.working: 2^10 = 1,024 layers x 0.1 mm = 10.2 cm. 2^30 = 1,073,741,824 layers x 0.1 mm = 107 km, above the 100 km Karman line.
science.source: arithmetic; Karman line (FAI definition of the edge of space, 100 km)
science.status: arithmetic checked; re-check the Karman line source

science.claim: By hand about seven folds is the limit, and the record is twelve.
science.working: Seven folds was the commonly accepted limit; 12 folds is the Guinness World Record, made with a tissue-paper roll about 1,219 m long.
science.source: Guinness World Records, 22 Oct 2025; Live Science
science.status: verified; do not name the record holder (no claims about real people)
